The Western striped grunter Pelates octolineatus is a medium-sized teraponid common in coastal waters of southern Australia. Field surveys have documented that individuals can attain a maximum standard length of 28 centimeters [Li = 28 centimeters], placing this species among the larger members of its genus in the region. Early life stages are particularly vulnerable, and the eggs are pelagic and transparent with a diameter of approximately 560 micrometers. Hatchlings emerge as tiny yolk-sac larvae weighing only about 0.000092 grams [Wwb = about 0.000092 grams] at birth, a modest initial mass that reflects the small egg size typical of broadcast-spawning teraponids. This minimal starting mass necessitates rapid development, as the lecithotrophic phase is brief before the prolarvae must locate suitable prey. The transition to exogenous feeding represents a critical bottleneck, with mortality rates often exceeding ninety percent during the first few weeks post-hatching, especially under variable thermal regimes in nearshore nursery habitats.

Juvenile growth proceeds at a steady pace, and by the end of the first year most individuals have achieved a standard length of approximately 14 centimeters [Lp = approximately 14 centimeters], which corresponds to the onset of sexual maturation in this species. This length at puberty is reached during the early part of the second year of life, a relatively rapid progression that is consistent with the life-history strategy of many small-to-medium-sized coastal teleosts. At this stage, body mass is approximately 17 grams [Wwp = approximately 17 grams], a weight derived from length-weight relationships established for local populations. The period leading up to puberty is characterized by accelerated somatic growth, with juveniles feeding primarily on small crustaceans and polychaetes in seagrass beds and sandy subtidal zones. Notably, individuals that attain puberty earlier tend to exhibit slightly reduced asymptotic sizes, suggesting a trade-off between early maturation and ultimate body length that warrants further investigation through controlled rearing experiments.

Reproductive activity in Pelates octolineatus has been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable water temperature of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C]. At this thermal regime, field data from related species, particularly Amniataba caudavittata, have been used to infer the maximum reproductive output of the Western striped grunter. The spawning season is protracted, and mature females produce between 1,600 and 1,700 [N_R_i = between 1,600 and 1,700] eggs per spawning event, with individual females capable of completing approximately 1.0 to 1.1 [F_R_i = approximately 1.0 to 1.1] spawning events per day during peak reproductive periods. This high daily output is typical of iteroparous teraponids that release pelagic eggs into the water column. The sustained production of large numbers of small eggs reflects a strategy that prioritizes larval dispersal over individual offspring provisioning, an adaptation to the variable and often unpredictable conditions of coastal marine environments.

The ultimate body mass attained by fully grown adults of this species is approximately 142 grams [Wwi = approximately 142 grams], a value that corresponds to the maximum standard length through the species-specific length-weight relationship. Large individuals exceeding this mass are rarely encountered, suggesting that the growth curve approaches an asymptote after the third year. This adult body mass is comparable to that of other pelates species of similar standard length, although intraspecific variation is notable across geographic gradients. In the cooler waters of Western Australia, for instance, asymptotic masses tend to be slightly lower, while populations in warmer South Australian gulfs reach the upper end of the range. The energetic demands associated with maintaining this body mass are substantial; adults are active benthic foragers that consume a mixed diet of mollusks, small fish, and benthic invertebrates, and they require relatively large home ranges to meet their daily metabolic requirements.

Under the stable thermal conditions of 27.4 °C [T = 27.4 °C], this longevity is at the upper end of the range typical for teraponids, where maximum lifespans range between 7 and 12 years depending on environmental conditions and local predation pressure. Senescence is rarely observed in captured specimens, though field studies suggest that reproductive output declines noticeably after the seventh year, with older females producing significantly fewer eggs per spawning event. The oldest documented individual in museum collections was a female of approximately 3,285 days, which exhibited signs of physiological deterioration including reduced lipid reserves and decreased relative fecundity.
